item.mechanism: Mn preferentially diffuses to the surface due to its high diffusion rate and high oxygen affinity, reacting with available oxygen to form non-protective Mn oxides, which depletes the bulk alloy of Mn.
item.system: CrMnFeCoNi equiatomic high-entropy alloy (20 at.% each)
item.operating_conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air (1.0 atm) and vacuum (4.2 × 10⁻⁶ atm) up to 1100 °C
item.supporting_observation: EDS line scans showed high Mn counts in the oxide scale dipping near the surface; Mn-rich outer layers and Mn-depleted zones were observed in cross-sections.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for Cr₂O₃ or Fe₂O₃ formation; the mechanism relies on Mn's diffusion rate being two orders faster than Cr, which may vary in other alloys.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of protective Cr₂O₃ or Fe-oxides was considered but not observed; thermodynamic predictions suggested Ni/Co oxides which were not found.
quotes: Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn
Mn has a higher affinity for oxygen, with an increase in temperature, Mn preferentially diffuses from inside to the surface and thus reacts with oxygen

item.mechanism: In vacuum conditions with low oxygen partial pressure, Mn oxidizes to form MnO (halite structure) exclusively because the low oxygen availability prevents the formation of higher oxides or mixed spinels.
item.supporting_observation: XRD patterns showed only MnO peaks; EDS mapping confirmed the oxide scale was solely an Mn-oxide layer with no other oxides.
item.scope_limits: Does not apply to atmospheric conditions where Mn₂O₃ and spinels form; the mechanism is specific to the low oxygen partial pressure regime.
item.alternatives_considered: Thermodynamic calculations predicted spinel oxides and NiO/CoO halites, but these were not observed experimentally.
quotes: The new peaks during phase identification were found to be MnO, and the substrate material conserved its phase stability throughout up to 1100 °C
The EDS mapping results show that the oxide scale formed in a vacuum is solely an Mn-oxide layer with no other type of oxides
This study validates MnO formation due to the lower oxygen partial pressure

item.mechanism: In air, Mn oxidizes initially to Mn₂O₃ (corundum structure) at lower temperatures, which then transforms into Mn₃O₄ (spinel) at higher temperatures (950 °C) as Mn₂O₃ is consumed to form mixed oxides.
item.operating_conditions: Air environment (1.0 atm) heated from room temperature to 1100 °C
item.supporting_observation: XRD showed Mn₂O₃ peaks appearing at 550 °C, weakening at 900 °C, and vanishing after 950 °C as Mn₃O₄ peaks appeared.
item.scope_limits: The transformation sequence is time- and temperature-dependent; the mechanism assumes sufficient oxygen availability which differs from vacuum.
item.alternatives_considered: The formation of stable binary Cr₂O₃ was considered but not detected; the authors note that the absence of Cr₂O₃ allows further Mn diffusion.
quotes: At 950 °C, Mn 3 O 4 starts to form as small new peaks and as it consumes the peaks belonging to Mn 2 O 3
The disappearance of Mn 2 O 3 is caused by the rapid consumption of Mn 2 O 3 for the generation of the mixed oxides of Mn 3 O 4 , MnCr 2 O 4 , and Mn 3 Fe 3 O 8

item.mechanism: The formation of ternary spinel oxides (MnCr₂O₄, Mn₃Fe₃O₈) occurs because Cr and Fe diffuse outward and combine with Mn and oxygen, rather than forming their own stable binary oxides like Cr₂O₃.
item.operating_conditions: Air environment (1.0 atm) at temperatures between 800 °C and 1100 °C
item.supporting_observation: XRD identified MnCr₂O₄ at 800 °C and Mn₃Fe₃O₈ at higher temperatures; EDS showed a Cr-rich inner layer beneath the Mn-rich outer layer.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to the short-to-medium timescale of the in situ experiment; the authors suggest binary oxides might form after longer exposure.
item.alternatives_considered: The formation of Cr₂O₃ was expected based on literature but was not detected; the authors attribute this to the rapid formation of Mn oxides.
quotes: Mixed oxide phases were identified during in situ XRD in the form of Mn 3 Fe 3 O 8 , and MnCr 2 O 4 , which signals that the surface and diffused-out Cr and Fe combined with Mn and oxygen to form ternary oxides
It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr 2 O 3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn

item.mechanism: The absence of a protective Cr₂O₃ layer prevents the inhibition of Mn diffusion, leading to the continuous growth of a non-protective, thick Mn-rich oxide scale.
item.operating_conditions: Air environment (1.0 atm) at high temperatures (up to 1100 °C)
item.supporting_observation: The oxide scale in air was thick (1.58–3.45 μm) and inhomogeneous, contrasting with the thin scale in vacuum; no Cr₂O₃ peaks were detected in XRD.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically to the CrMnFeCoNi system where Cr₂O₃ does not form; it may not transfer to alloys where Cr₂O₃ is stable.
item.alternatives_considered: The formation of a protective Cr₂O₃ barrier was considered a standard mechanism for high-temperature alloys but was explicitly ruled out by the experimental data.
quotes: As no Cr-rich oxide of the form Cr 2 O 3 formed during the oxidation test to work as a barrier and inhibit or slow down the diffusion of Mn element, no protection of the substrate beneath the scale to further oxidation was thus available
The presence of a uniform and protective oxide scale serves to impede the continued oxidation of the underlying materials

item.mechanism: Thermodynamic equilibrium calculations (CALPHAD) predict spinel oxides in air and halite oxides in vacuum, but these predictions fail to account for kinetic limitations that favor MnO and Mn₂O₃ formation over predicted Ni/Co oxides.
item.operating_conditions: Equilibrium conditions simulated at 1000 °C and 1100 °C with varying oxygen partial pressures
item.supporting_observation: ThermoCalc predicted NiO and CoO as major halite oxides in vacuum and spinel oxides in air, but experiments showed only MnO in vacuum and Mn/Cr/Fe spinels in air.
item.scope_limits: The thermodynamic model assumes equilibrium and does not account for kinetics, diffusion rates, or the specific timescale of the experiment.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that the discrepancy might be due to the time scale required to reach the most stable equilibrium state.
quotes: ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results
Thermodynamic calculations focus on equilibrium conditions and do not account for the kinetics of reactions
Such a discrepancy in results between the ThermoCalc-predicted oxide types (i.e., NiO, CoO) and the experimentally found one (MnO only) could be the time scale

item.mechanism: Mn depletion in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer occurs due to the outward diffusion of Mn, which negatively impacts the mechanical properties by reducing solid solution strengthening.
item.operating_conditions: High-temperature exposure (up to 1100 °C) in air and vacuum
item.supporting_observation: EDS maps showed Mn-depleted zones at the scale-substrate interface; the authors link this to the loss of mechanical strength.
item.scope_limits: This effect is specific to alloys where Mn is a major strengthening element; the extent of depletion depends on the oxidation duration and temperature.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect of HEAs might be reduced by the depletion of elements like Mn.
quotes: Mn is known to contribute to solid solution strengthening and can enhance the mechanical strength and ductility of alloys
The formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures
Mn depletion creates doubt about the application of HEA for high-temperature applications and due to the higher diffusion rate may affect the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect

item.mechanism: The in situ HTXRD technique reveals real-time phase transformations (e.g., Mn₂O₃ to Mn₃O₄) that are missed by post-mortem analysis, which often assumes phase stability at ambient temperature.
item.operating_conditions: In situ heating from 25 °C to 1100 °C in air and vacuum
item.supporting_observation: The study observed the transient existence of Mn₂O₃ which vanished at 950 °C, a transformation not captured by standard post-oxidation analysis.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to the capability of the in situ technique; it does not describe a material property but rather an observation method that corrects previous assumptions.
item.alternatives_considered: Previous studies based on post-mortem analysis assumed different oxidation products (e.g., Cr₂O₃) which were contradicted by the real-time data.
quotes: Clearly, this introduces a degree of uncertainty, since one cannot be completely sure of the underlying physical mechanisms which are imperative on the critical scales
Time–temperature-resolved in situ XRD observations would be invaluable in circumventing this ambiguity and in elucidating the chemical processes giving rise to the oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi alloy
Our study shows that the in situ HTXRD technique is a powerful tool to accurately identify time–temperature-dependent phase formation/transformation
